narrative:
The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

The decision was driven mainly by three key factors. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence, but it pulled the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay have similar short experience levels, so this actually worked in your favor. 

What pushed the prediction upward were the other two important factors. Having received other job offers while working here strongly increased the likelihood of leaving. In contrast, most people the model predicts will stay have not received such external opportunities. Second, working in the “other” sector also raised the chance of departure. Only about 22% of employees predicted to stay work in this broad category, while the majority are in medical or education roles that the model associates with greater stability.

Taken together, these signals led the system to conclude you are more likely to leave than not. The organization should discuss your external opportunities and sector-specific challenges with you openly. You might consider what would make staying more attractive, such as clearer growth paths or additional support, before making any decisions.
